speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I wish to bring this matter to the attention of the house and the country because of a statement issued by the Prime Minister this morning over the C.B.C. with regard to legislative matters to be brought before this house, and because of a presentation that was made in a non-political fashion to the members of parliament shortly before the opening of the house today.

DECISION ON SHOWING OF FILM ON PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have received the decision made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on the film entitled "Mr. Pearson" and I should like to communicate it to the house. It is as follows:
The directors of the corporation at their annual meeting have carefully reviewed those aspects of the rejected television film "Mr. Pearson" which are directly its concern:
(1)	The broadcasting or professional decision not to show the film, and
(2)	Whether compelling factors now exist which would outweigh the corporation's operational standards and judgment.
The corporation has made its decision on the basis of the full responsibility in programming matters delegated to it by parliament. There are three basic elements in the decision:
(1)	The film remains unacceptable for showing on the basis of broadcast standards.
(2)	The corporation is satisfied there has been no political interference.
(3)	Though an interest in the film has been stimulated in segments of the public, nevertheless the corporation does not judge the broadcasting of the film to be warranted.
The corporation's decision is not to show the film or parts thereof.

Mr. Chairman, there was
something rather grotesque in the concentration of the house yesterday upon the Pearson film. I think it has been made even more grotesque by the decision of the C.B.C. today. I do not intend to carry on the discussion, but I want to place some questions before the Prime Minister. Yesterday the Prime Minister indicated that this was his first opportunity to speak in full on this matter. I think he started well, but in so far as the fulsomeness of the explanation was concerned, he began to run out well before the end of his speech.
I do not believe we will have a full explanation. I would predict, as a result of the repercussions within the structure of the C.B.C. that we have not heard the end of this. As a matter of fact it begins to look very much as though we have almost a duplicate of the "Preview Commentary" situation of a few years ago brewing. I hope if this should be the case we will have the matter referred to a committee rather more quickly than was the case at that time.
I wanted to raise this point with the Prime Minister. He indicated that there were two reasons why the film was screened for him and other members of his staff. One was the question, which I think we will all accept, of the secrecy of matters in relation to the cabinet and the Prime Minister's office. The other was the question of something that you may call good taste, that was the question of the personal selection that was involved in the television production.
I want to ask the Prime Minister this question. At the first showing did he have with him a professor from York University by the name of William Kilboum? I raise this question because I understand Professor Kilboum was with him. He is a man for whom I have a great deal of respect. As well as being a supporter of the Prime Minister he is considered somewhat of an authority on television, on the standards of television performance. I can quite understand that it might have been completely informal that Professor Kilboum wound up seeing this particular film. I happen to know-the Prime Minister may wonder

where I got the information, but I got it directly-that Professor Kilbourn had an opinion after seeing this film. He had an opinion upon its worth, not in connection with secrecy or the Prime Minister's personal taste but on the basis of whether it was good television and a good projection of the subject.
I think this is something that runs through the whole matter. Many members of the house know that the national director of the Liberal party happens to be a friend of mine of long standing. I want to raise the issue that he was included also in the screenings that were given of this film. I ask the Prime Minister, how does this square with the two matters, the question of personal taste and the question of secrecy? I suggest to the Prime Minister that yesterday in his speech when he got toward the end he missed out entirely on the explanation for all the screenings.
I can only assume from his performance yesterday that he has what I can only call in order to get around the need for a name, the man from Prince Albert syndrome. He is obsessed, in some way, with the position and attitude of the Leader of the Opposition. It was revealed in his speech yesterday. For some reason this does not allow him to be completely open and direct about the details in connection with this particular film.
Put it in your column.

The Prime Minister has made a number of references to my column and television show. I appreciate these very much, but I am speaking here as a parliamentarian very closely watching this particular situation develop, and in connection with this film I want to ask the Prime Minister if he can see the possibilities in this light.
For some reason he withdrew his own personal judgment in connection with the matter some time before that final screening attended by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. For some reason the Prime Minister decided that he would leave the judgment to these colleagues of his and to those associates of his within his own office. I do not know why he did this, but I would ask him whether he can tell me in all candidness that these gentlemen did not form a judgment upon the merit of the film as it affected him as Prime Minister and leader of the Liberal party, and whether that judgment-I am not saying to the Prime Minister's knowledge it was communicated deliberately- whether he really believes that judgment made by that group or those associated with
Interim Supply
him was not given to Reeves Haggan, the director of public affairs of the C.B.C.
I would like to point out to the Prime Minister that his explanation yesterday began to run out of detail just where the Dennis Braithwaite descriptions of the incident began to get to grips with what I think are some very important things. I just want to take this extract from the second column and draw it to the Prime Minister's attention:
In about half an hour,
-this is after the screening-
Mr. Ballentine and Mr. Haggan were called to Mr. O'Hagan's office, where they were told that everyone thought highly of the film. Tom Kent called it brilliant. However, it must be understood that there was some concern about it from a publicity and political point of view.
Mr. Haggan said he thought it was sympathetic to the Prime Minister.
In other words Mr. Haggan, the director of public affairs, was arguing that the film should be accepted, that there should be some kind of seal of approval.
There is only one thing I could draw from this kind of group passing approval on it, and I am suggesting we have not had a clear explanation from the Prime Minister as to whether the judgment of this group, on this question of publicity from a political point of view, was not given to Mr. Haggan; and I would suggest, as I did two days ago, that Mr. Haggan as a good executive and good employee of the C.B.C. almost certainly let this opinion be known to his senior officials. I think this is the only explanation one can get of just what transpired, and I think the Prime Minister should tell us whether he does not believe this is possible, that this is likely.
We are prepared to accept the Prime Minister's statement that he was not guilty of political interference, but surely in the light of the two points he was trying to bring out all through yesterday's debate that he felt he had the right-and indeed he behaved as if he had the right, and he delegated the right to his associates-to judge the film on the question of his personal tastes and personal affairs and on the whole question of whether it was secret or not, he must realize that this spreads out and makes possible the judging of that film on the basis of what Mr. Braithwaite has called the publicity and political points of view.
I do not know whether we are going to get a key answer but I suggest that the Prime Minister-I shall not say would be well advised because that is presumptuous- might take it up with his staff and see

Interim Supply
whether it was not accurate that Mr. Haggan, the senior man in C.B.C. relations respecting this film, was aware ol the views on the part of the Prime Minister's associates to whom he delegated or apparently delegated the judgment, that they felt the film would be a poor one to show because of the publicity and political problems inherent in it.
The last point I want to make in connection with the Pearson film concerns the decision that the C.B.C. has taken not to show it. They have the right to make that decision, but I think it is a wrong one on two counts. Having seen the film I cannot accept that it is bad technically, that it is below normal C.B.C. standards. To my mind it was well above the C.B.C. technical standards, but that is my personal opinion.
I know there will continue to be an interest in this film. I would not like to suggest that the house should get into the position of asking the C.B.C. to go any further so far as putting it on television is concerned, but I certainly think that in the minds of almost all members of the house the whole question will not be at rest until they have an opportunity to view the film. I would like to suggest that some of us should make an arrangement to form a film society, because Mr. Braithwaite has prints, and I suggest that the Prime Minister would do very well, in the light of these people's comments, if he would become the honourary patron of the House of Commons film society. I am suggesting this with a certain amount of humour, but I hope we actually form a society so that we can see the film. I want to see it shown to back up what I have said on the record, that it is a brilliant film, technically excellent, and should be shown to the Canadian people; and I want my associates in the house, not only my associates over here but also on the other side, to form their judgment.
There is one other matter I want to touch on very briefly, a matter that may in a sense be related to this. This party I represent is very disappointed over the failure of the house to come up with some limitation upon debate, some formal arrangement. It is not proper for me to make any comments on the operations of a committee of the house, a committee that is presently sitting, but we are disappointed that that committee has not brought forward recommendations so we could have a means of negotiating limitation of debate.
On this point I would express some views to the official opposition. If it considers fairly,

it will agree that minor parties in the house have more to lose from a limitation upon debate than the official opposition itself. The Leader of the Opposition has unlimited time to speak. He has the first opportunity to speak, and in any kind of ratio we have worked out in recent years the official opposition of the day, whether the Liberal party in opposition or the Conservative party in opposition, has done well-I will not say unfairly well, but fairly well-in the ratio of speakers. I put it to the official opposition that if anything the people who should worry about a restriction and time limit on debate, particularly on legislation, are the members of our party and our colleagues to our left.
I would ask the official opposition, particularly the Leader of the Opposition, in appraising this matter which I think is the most vital before parliament in so far as parliament's own good health is concerned, that they look more favourably than they have so far on this question of limiting debate. I think it is absolutely essential if we are going to resurrect the health and I think the life, if you want, of an institution that is not very favourably situated at the present time. Even if we do not think so, many people out in the country feel this is so.
We would like to close our remarks-and I say "we" because I am speaking for my colleagues-by putting to the Prime Minister that we feel he has not taken a strong hand in leading discussions and in presenting possibilities in connection with the matter of limitations upon debate. We can understand the fear which exists in the mind of any alert politician with regard to the whole question of closure in the light of what happened in 1956 and thereafter, but I should like to point out to the right hon. gentleman how much the climate and attitude have changed since then. I remember in 1957 arguing with my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that we needed limitation of debate negotiated in the same way as in the British parliament. He disagreed very strongly with me. He felt this was really a denial of what we were setting out to do. I think it will be agreed that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has changed his mind. He now feels as I do on this question, which is perhaps the most vital of all the points to be considered in connection with the reform of parliament.
I suggest that the Prime Minister has never, except in the loosest or vaguest way, put forward anything in the nature of a formula or plan by which we could move toward this

objective. He is probably saying "Why should I get involved in something like that?"
We have done so. We set up a committee.
When has the Prime Minister ever put forward publicly and in this house an effective way of doing it? I have not seen it or heard of it.

Perhaps the hon. member would allow me to answer that question now. I put forward four proposals to expedite and make more effective parliamentary procedure when we were in opposition in the last parliament. I put those four proposals forward after we formed the government. I advanced a proposal to set up a committee to look into parliamentary procedure. We put a cabinet minister to sit on that committee with instructions that he should support every proposal which would expedite and make more effective the business of this house.
Well, in our opinion that has not been enough, and I will tell the right hon. gentleman one of the reasons.
You blocked every motion.
This is the key. What we need in this problem is good faith.
Hear, hear.
We need good faith in connection with this matter and the Prime Minister, as the senior person in this house, has not been able to engender that good faith.
Quite right.

I say this is a responsibility which rests upon him. It is not enough for him to say he has put forward four proposals. If this parliament wishes to achieve these objectives, something more aggressive has to be done and, I suggest, something much more friendly than the Prime Minister has come forward with as yet.
I should also like to suggest something further. If we are to get over these limitations and if we cannot get co-operation after a fair effort, then another responsibility rests upon the Prime Minister; that is to begin to consider other means by which the results can be achieved.
Quite right. Put it on the order paper.

You extend the hours of sitting. I remember I myself once had the honour of having a motion accepted in this house to
Interim Supply
extend the hours of sitting, and the right hon. gentleman will remember what happened as a result. We just got the longest Hansard in history, and I do not think we got out of here any sooner. I am wondering whether the same thing is likely to happen as far this motion is concerned.
My proposition on behalf of this party is twofold. First, we want more co-operation from the Prime Minister in working on this problem, and if no solution is apparent in the next few weeks we think the Prime Minister then has to begin to consider the other steps -and I think they are obvious; I think we have a tradition in this regard-
Will the hon. member tell us what they are?
They have existed since the time of the debate on the naval bill before the first world war.
Bring in closure?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: You are not speaking for all of us now.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre "You are not speaking for all of us now".
Oh, oh.
You have a split, eh?
Can they settle their dispute between them before they tell us what the policy is?

The point here is that I am not taking it upon myself or upon my colleagues to set out a policy. I am suggesting that if the Prime Minister, who has the power, wants to achieve the legislative program he talks about there is an ultimate responsibility upon him-
That is not very friendly.

An hon. gentleman says it would not be very friendly, but that is the challenge to the Prime Minister. It is he who has undertaken to get through this legislative program. It is not moving very well. He is having a great time blaming everybody else, and I suggest that if he cannot obtain the kind of co-operation which results from negotiation on the basis of good faith then he has to consider other means, whether friendly or not, of achieving his purpose-
Oh, oh.

The very reaction one gets in connection with this subject indicates the timidity in the thinking of hon. members over there. It is not the responsibility of members of the opposition to suggest the

Interim Supply
introduction of closure, but I say it is about time this government began to think about doing something like that.
Oh, oh.
Let us put it this way.
I object. I object.
How about a caucus?

Obviously I have not been exact in my phrasing. I want to make it very clear that there is a responsibility vested in the Prime Minister to get the business through this house. The Prime Minister has been having a fine time blaming everyone else for the slowness with which we have proceeded. I should like to suggest that if he cannot achieve the reforms which many of us feel are needed, he should consider those other responsibilities which rest upon him.
What?
I have already indicated what those other measures are. Never mind. I am very sorry if my colleagues fear that I was advocating closure.
Oh, oh.

Well, let us consider the other possibility. What is this other possibility? It is the dissolution of this parliament and the holding of an election. Those are the three possibilities. I personally-this is a personal preference-would prefer the third one, because I am not convinced that this government or this Prime Minister are ever going to act with the kind of resolution which would enable them to use the other thing in this connection. I just want to leave this issue before the house as a whole, this being a debate in which anyone can discuss the matter, because I think it is very obvious that we are fighting back and forth without really achieving the legislative program we should.
Just before 2.30 today a number of us met with a group of Canadian students, members of the Canadian union of students who are anxious to have certain legislation put forward. I am not trying to read anything into their attitude, but it appeared to me they were cynical and sceptical to a marked extent about the capacity of this parliament to get on with this legislation and get it through in any reasonable time. I suggest that when an attitude of this sort is abroad in the country among such a group as this, the Prime Minister should begin seriously to consider means of getting down to the implementation

of measures such as the student loan bill, because it is evident that parliament is not handling these things very quickly.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Does he have in mind the statement made by the Minister of Finance on a national television broadcast, when he said "the Liberal party has the program and the platform and we think we have the leader"?
I do not think I need to comment on that. I believe the house knows my views.

I should like to take a few moments of the time of the committee in order to comment on the extraordinary situation I witnessed a few moments ago. I listened to an hon. member saying that he did not want to take very much upon himself. It seemed to me that he had taken a great deal upon himself in giving advice when he evidently did not even have the support of his own party.
Everyone in this group has the support of the party.

In that particular group over there it would seem that if there is one man who does not have their support, it is their deputy leader. He talked about co-operation, and as I watched the reaction of his colleagues there seemed to be a great lack of coordination in their view. The point I would like to make is one that I think is valid, because the hon. member, unlike myself or my colleagues over here, has a great forum across this nation and he has pontificated on a great many subjects ad infinitum and occasionally ad nauseam.
I would just like to use this opportunity to draw particular attention to the contradictions and inadequacies of his remarks and to point to what I think is the most crucial point, namely that he is a man who is an independent member and does not really understand the problems of leadership. It is almost like-and I use this by way of analogy -a deaf mute sitting down lip reading a great oration. He can try to write about it, but unless you listen to an oration you cannot appreciate it. I think this represents an analogy to the hon. member for Port Arthur and shows the invalidity of his comments today.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before saying a word or two concerning what the hon.

member for Port Arthur said I want to refer to an incident in the debate of yesterday when there was an incomplete reporting in Hansard of something that I said. I would like to put the record straight. The Prime Minister was talking about the difficulty of secret conversations appearing on the film, and as reported at page 4681 of Hansard I asked him this question, which is reported incompletely:
What secret conversations could you have, as a member of the privy council, in the presence of outsiders?
Because of the commotion in the house the latter part of the question was omitted. The Prime Minister replied that he would be very glad to answer that question and went on to say:
There were conversations in my office with cabinet ministers and we talked about public policy.
The point I was making was simply this, that the Prime Minister has admitted that members of the privy council, subject to the privy council oath, talked about matters of public policy in the presence of outsiders. Because he had done that, and because these conversations were recorded on tape, he wanted the right to excise them from the final version of the film, in the interests of security. In the interests of security these subjects should never have been talked about by members of the privy council in the presence of outsiders.
This surely is a gross dereliction of duty and responsibility, and I thought the Prime Minister failed to give an adequate explanation to the house yesterday with regard to that matter. I have been wondering since, what about these sections of the film that I understand have been cut out of the final production, which nobody is to see now? What about these sections which have recorded permanently secret conversations among members of the privy council on matters of public policy? Who has these sections of the film? In whose possession are they? Into whose hands will they fall?
The communists.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
This is a very grave situation indeed, Mr. Chairman, and I wonder why the Prime Minister failed to give a more adequate explanation of those secret conversations of privy councillors. I wish to make that extension and correction of Hansard because I was inadequately reported yesterday. I do not propose pursuing that subject at the moment, although there is plenty one could say 20220-299
Interim Supply
with regard to the inadequate explanation of the Prime Minister.
I would like to talk for just a few minutes about what the hon. member for Port Arthur has said. He is in effect asking for the regimentation of this free institution. He wants everything put in a strait-jacket. He is in favour of curtailing freedom of speech. He is advocating closure. I say this because he referred to the naval debate of 1913. What was the purpose of referring to that unless he was asking the Prime Minister to put into effect what was done at that time? Then in 1956 we had another example of the curtailment of debate.
I am surprised that the deputy leader of the New Democratic party would be advocating the curtailment of speech in this house. No party has made better use of the freedom this institution provides than that party. The members of the New Democratic party time and time again have made use of the time of this house to present their views. In days gone by I well recall filibusters by members of that party week after week on subjects that were before this house, and there was no curtailment of the right of speech.
Timiskaming and Skeena.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
There was no closure applied. The hon. member for Port Arthur was talking about the public image of this institution. I do not know why members of parliament are trying to destroy the image of this institution by constantly condemning it in public. Let them make their statements here in the house-and I welcome the statement he made this morning-and not outside, so we can have a debate on the subject and can reply to such statements. But going outside this house, talking to high school students and other people and saying this is a sick parliament and that the institution has something faulty about it, does a great deal of harm. What are you doing? You are tearing down something that has centuries of tradition and prestige behind it. This is where the flame of freedom glows in Canada, right here in this chamber. There is no suppression of news here, except by those who do not want to give the full facts.
This is where every subject under the sun can be discussed. There is no curtailment of the important news of the country, as happened on the C.B.C. the other night when there was no mention of the fact that parliament was in session. This is the institution that preserves the liberties of the subject. Here is where you have freedom of speech,

Interim, Supply
and now the hon. member wants to curtail it. I ask him, for what purpose?
To get down to the business.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
He said "Let us operate the way they do in the House of Commons at Westminster, where debates are curtailed". Debates in the House of Commons at Westminster are shortened on some occasions by mutual agreement, just as has been done here for years and will continue, I hope, to be done here for years. There is no curtailment of debate in the British House of Commons except by the action of the Speaker, who has greater authority than the Speaker has been given in the Canadian House of Commons. He can, when it comes to the amendment of legislation, accept some amendments and reject others on his own authority. There are certain over-all time limits spent on some aspects of parliamentary business at Westminster, just as we have over-all time limits on the speech from the throne, the budget debate and on supply motions, and within those limits we attempt to operate.
The British House of Commons does not impose a time limit on legislation very often. It is only on average once in two years, on occasions when they have a very controversial piece of legislation in front of them and which they feel they must under the circumstances pass, that the government imposes an allocation of time and there is restriction of debate. This is normally undertaken only after reaching the committee of the whole house stage, after the house has spent several days debating the subject in question. It is not normal practice at all, and it is ridiculous for people to suggest that we should be doing here what they do there as if it was normal practice in the British House of Commons. It is not so at all.
The British house introduced allocation of time back in the days when the Irish nationalists were obstructing the parliament of Great Britain and brought things to a dead stop. Allocation of time was first imposed on two bills affecting Ireland introduced into the House of Commons by Balfour, who was secretary of state for Ireland. That is when they started, and that system of allocation of time has persisted in the British house and was used more frequently during that period and up to the 1930's than it has been since. It is not a popular measure in the British House of Commons. If you were to read the debates over recent years since the second world war, on occasions when alloca-

tion of time was applied with regard to legislation, every party in the house at one time or other, Conservative, Liberal and Labour, when forming the government applied an allocation of time order; and each one of those parties when in opposition has resisted the application of such an order. speechtext: The fifth.

If we go back a few years we will find from the evidence of the record that rarely did such a debate occupy more than a day. In fact, it was very often over in an hour or two. We have discussed at length the film "Mr. Pearson". It seems to me we ought to come back to just a little more sense of balance and understand that it is our particular responsibility at this time to authorize the expenditure of certain moneys for the carrying on of the

administration of the government and our country.
Hear, hear.

We should let this film matter go by the way for a little while and accept the word that has been given by various members of this house in answer to charges that have been made against them, in the honourable way that we would expect our own word to be accepted. For this reason, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me it would be far more befitting our responsibilities if we were to come to an amiable conclusion of this debate, because obviously we are not debating the subject which is before us at all. I was going to answer the house leader of the official opposition and some of the remarks he made, because I disagree with a number of them; but let us leave that aside as well. Certainly no one can disagree with the fact that I have just mentioned, namely that our responsibility now is to authorize the expenditure for another month of the moneys needed by the government in their responsibilities of carrying on the administration of this country.
We may not have agreed with all the things said by the hon. member for Port Arthur in regard to facilitating the work of this house, but on the other hand we must certainly agree with his basic premise, that we are not making the progress that we should be making. This responsibility falls upon, not just the government, not just the official opposition, but upon all of us. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has inferred very specifically that the house leaders of the minor parties have been in some kind of liaison or behind the scenes plot to work against the official opposition. I do not agree with this; I do not think it is true at all. Many remarks have been made recently to the effect that the fact this house of minorities is not making progress is the fault of the minor parties. This is not true at all. When the house leaders of the minor parties do come together in an effort to facilitate the work of the house, I am convinced they do so with a real depth of sincerity and, shall I say, patriotism, to try and make this house of minorities work. I say it can work if we make up our minds that it will work. It is not good enough just to be harping back to Westminster to try and show that they do not do things any differently than we do, or that they do things differently than we do. Our responsibility now is to each other and it is also to the nation, because there is important legislation on the order paper, waiting to be dealt with. The way we have been carrying on these past four days is certainly neither

to the credit of anybody in this house, nor to the advantage of anybody in this house-because we are the ones who are the final losers, as well as the country.
Are you speaking for yourself?

Yes, I am speaking for myself. For four days we have listened patiently to the carryings on of this house without making any remarks at all, because it seemed there was already too much being said.
I would appeal to hon. members present today to think upon these things. It is not a question of throwing sticks or stones, as an editorial in today's Globe and Mail points out; it is a question of facing up, in an honourable and responsible way, to the things we have been given the responsibility of doing. It is not a question, as I have just mentioned, of looking back to the past to try to justify our present shortcomings and sins. Rather it seems to me, we should take our hats off to the past, but take our coats off to the future and settle down and get to work.

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, June 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Brown for the second reading of Bill No. S-27, respecting The Bell Telephone Company of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: I should caution the house that if the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) speaks now he will close the debate.

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not usual to have the Bell Telephone Company before parliament, and when we do I think we should take the opportunity to ask a few questions about the company. I understand that this bill is to increase from 15 to 20 the maximum permissible number of directors. I think the time has arrived that we should look at the Bell Telephone Company in particular, as the largest telephone company in the nation, and the other telephone companies, with a view to incorporating them as a public utility to be operated for the good of the nation.
Telephones are a part of the same field of communication which includes radio, television, telegraph lines and so on. The telephone is used by everybody across the nation in the course of their daily activities. The Bell Telephone Company has been able to exercise tremendous control over the rights of the individual and in my opinion these rights have

quite often been abused by the corporation. In Canada we have a large microwave communications system extending from coast to coast which is owned by the telephone companies of Canada. About 25 per cent of its operations are for purposes of television broadcasting, and a considerable proportion is used for communication purposes by the army, navy and air force.
The telephone has become a vital necessity in the carrying on of the affairs of the nation not only in a military sense but in the business and personal life of the people. I believe that in amending this act we should also include an amendment to provide for the expropriation of the Bell Telephone Company so that, like most other communications media, it will come directly under the control of the federal government.
There are many abuses to which people are subjected by the Bell Telephone Company. Some of these abuses have come to my attention since I have been a resident of southern Ontario, because in northern Ontario we have a different telephone company and the same rules do not apply. I am informed that many arbitrary acts are perpetrated by the Bell Telephone Company in its relations with the general public. If the company wishes to do so it will supply a telephone to an applicant, but if it does not wish to supply a telephone it does not do so. If it wishes to impose a surcharge on a particular line it does so. If a bill is overdue several days the company has been known to cut off the telephone service, although the person may have an exceptionally good credit rating. This has been done several times in the rooming house where I live. It is caused partly by the fact that several persons use the telephone, with the result that the bills are quite large and cannot be apportioned until such time as they arrive at the house. Of course, the company charges an extra $5 to reconnect the telephone. They do not give the normal 30 days for the payment of a bill which is usually extended to those with a good credit rating. Instead they adopt an arbitrary attitude and may cut off the telephone within two or three days with or without warning.
In my opinion the company has used methods that are not conducive to the good and the welfare of the nation. Therefore I believe the time has arrived when we should put the telephone system under the control of the federal government in the same way that other communications media are being operated as public utilities at the present time. There are probably many who have

had an extended connection with the Bell Telephone Company and know more about it than I do. However, I would request an amendment that would provide not only for this company but other telephone companies as well to be brought under public ownership.
I hope that the bill will be referred to a committee. I presume it will and I hope that consideration will be given by members of the committee to a discussion of the merits of whether or not this particular amendment should be granted to the Bell Telephone Company and whether or not it will prove to be in the interests of the people of Canada. The argument may be made, of course, that this does not come within the purview of this amendment. This is perfectly true, but the Bell Telephone Company has a federal charter and therefore it is our responsibility to consider the broader aspects of its operations whenever an opportunity arises as the result of the introduction of amendments. I hope that the sponsor will ask that the bill be referred to a committee so that some consideration can be given to present problems and the advantages that Canada would obtain if the Bell Telephone Company were brought under public ownership in the same way as other communications media which operate under the control and direction of the federal government.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks I should like to make on the bill. In reading its language certain questions arise in my mind. First of all, I should like to know if the majority of directors at the present time are Canadians. I should also like to raise the question whether or not all of the directors should be Canadian, in an organization of this type dealing with communications in this country. Generally speaking there is no reason to raise a question of this kind in regard to many of our commercial organizations, but when communications are involved I think the question is a valid one. subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very simple bill. Its sole purpose is to increase from 15 to 20 the number of
Private Bills
directors provided in the act incorporating the company. I might point out to the house that in 1888, when the original bill was passed by parliament, the number of telephones in Canada was 14,550 while at December 31, 1963, there were over 4,090,000. I am referring to those operated by the Bell Telephone Company. In 1888 the total assets of this company amounted to $2,224,290 while at the end of 1963 their assets totalled $2,347,095,000.
In answer to the question of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) I should like to state that at December 31, 1963, the number of shareholders of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada was 195,037. Of this amount, the total number of Canadian shareholders was 189,718. The total number of shares owned by United States citizens was 3,969. The total number of shares owned by other foreign shareholders was 1,350. As can be seen, this is an almost wholly owned Canadian company. As a matter of fact 93.1 per cent of the capital stock is held by Canadians and 97.3 per cent of the shareholders were residents in Canada as at the end of December, 1963. The holding of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company as of December 31, 1963, was 2.8 per cent of the total number of shares.
These figures I have given the house in order to refute the statement made in the house by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) in the earlier debate on the bill. Further, in reply to the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden), I should like to state that' all the directors of the Bell Telephone Company except one; are Canadians; that is, 14 out of the 15 present directions are Canadian citizens. Only one director is a United States citizen and he is also a director of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company which holds 2.8 per cent of the stock. At the present time, therefore, all the directors but one are Canadian citizens. This is a very high proportion of directors who are Canadian citizens and a very high percentage of shareholders.
With these few explanatory remarks, Mr. Speaker, I shall draw my own remarks to a close and leave the bill to the discretion of the house.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack McIntosh (Swift Current-Maple Creek) moved
subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING WITHHOLDING OR REFUSAL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-39, to amend the Civil Service Act (bureaucratic oppression).
He said: Mr. Speaker, when I first introduced this bill in parliament I said, by way of explanation, that I had reason to believe some officials of the government, by virtue of their office, have on occasion intentionally deprived certain citizens of their rights declared under the provisions of Canadian statutes. I believe these officials have intentionally withheld those rights or refused the implementation of those rights until, in a given case, the citizen has bent to the official's will.

At present there is no penalty in the Civil Service Act for such bureaucratic oppression. This bill will provide a penalty if guilt for such action can be established. Perhaps I should have prefaced my remarks by saying any allegation I may make is not directed against the rank and file of the civil service, most of whom I believe are loyal, devoted and efficient public servants, but rather against the few who trample freedom and ride roughshod over individual rights. Generally speaking, I think I would agree that Canada has a high grade civil service, manned by personnel who are dedicated people, but a service that is handicapped by a system, a system badly needing revision, and one which in many ways represses initiative and favours the status quo.
It has been said that an administrator is a bureaucrat whose prime loyalty is to the public good; a bureaucrat is an administrator whose prime loyalty is to the administrative machine of which he is a cog. While I know that bureaucrats are necessary I also feel a number of them overemphasize their authority and at times eliminate justice. I am one of those who believe that public servants are the servants of the public and not the masters, as some seem to believe by their actions.
Many Canadians, I feel certain, could testify to at some time having suffered the embarrassment and humiliation of tangling with some dominating bureaucrat within our federal departments. If we allow trained, efficient civil servants to take over we get a bureaucracy, and democracy ceases to exist. This fact is a weakness in our democratic system, a weakness which we as members of parliament are charged to watch.
I have stated before and I will repeat that, no matter what party the taxpayers elect, no matter what government is in power, the bureaucratic dictators still run the country. To a large degree the government is a captive of the civil service, and the ministers are hostages to their deputies and senior departmental officials. Successive governments in the capital of our country have, without thought, or I should say without intent, gradually vacated certain areas of authority or responsibility which, in a democracy, should always be occupied by publicly elected officials or their representatives, leaving the departmental officials decisions which they have neither the practical training nor the mandate to exercise.
It may be a revelation to some Canadians, particularly to us members of parliament, to

find out for ourselves the degree to which civil servants have taken over the affairs of our country. As members of parliament I believe that two statements made by the high commissioner of New Zealand in a speech to the royal commonwealth society should be of interest to us. The first statement refers to travellers in his country, New Zealand, and the contact they have with people in that country. I think the same applies here in Canada:
Even lor the native inhabitants it will be found that the public servant has more effect on their lives than all the politicians, businessmen, church, law and press combined.
The second statement that I bring to hon. members' attention is this:
In France before de Gaulle, governments came and went three or four times a year, but the government of France by its highly organized public servants carried on, hardly aware of the changes.
Some hon. members may say this cannot happen in our country; but I wonder if it can. Just a few days ago a press item appeared in the Ottawa Journal regarding civil defence, and dealing with an appearance by a former deputy minister, now a minister of the crown, before the Commons special defence committee. It was in the issue of Friday June 19 and read as follows:
Mr. Drury was questioned in his statement that survival of government was ensured through special shelters, complete with essential records, and rapid transit to them of government officers and a selected 200 top officials, presumably to the four major underground bunkers in the Ottawa area.
He was asked by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Smith):
-where M.P.'s stood on the list of priorities for evacuation in an emergency-
And the hon. member was told:
-they were well down the list, since the plan was to evacuate "only important people."
In other words they do not feel that M.P.'s are important people. In fact lots of times I have felt that maybe we were a sort of nuisance so far as civil servants were concerned.
The article continues:
The laughter this prompted caused Mr. Drury to explain that the 200 officials were top ones "who work for the government"-
This apparently drew another laugh in the committee.
To me, this degree of influence by the civil servants is startling. As a member of parliament since 1958, I have become increasingly concerned about the number of times I have had to accept a ruling, or an answer from a departmental official without a means to
Private Bills
challenge the decision of the bureaucrat. At present there is no adequate parliamentary procedure available to a member of parliament to obtain redress for his constituents' grievances against an unjust ruling handed down by departmental officials, other than appealing to a very busy minister.
In the case of an individual citizen who comes into conflict with some government official, there does not exist for him any procedure whereby he can challenge the action of the executive. There are executives in fact who appear to have the sole power to interpret the act they are charged with administering, and do so without the risk of being penalized for any wrong action on their part. In a great many cases I would suggest the rights of the individuals are being sacrificed to the efficiency of government planners. I have stated previously that I believe the basic trouble lies in the fact that the government has allowed itself to become captive of the civil service, and the ministers are hostages to their deputies and senior departmental officials.
The most recent personal experience I encountered in this regard took place in the private members' hour on Tuesday June 16, when I endeavoured to pilot Bill C-37 through this house. It was talked out by government supporters, with the main excuse that it would be too difficult for the department to administer. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) brought this to the attention of the house when he said, as recorded at page 4366 of Hansard:
it-
-referring to Bill C-37-
-will not receive the attention it deserves because the spokesman for the government, the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pilon) raised the usual objections which come from officials. He said it would be difficult for the department to administer it; that it would be hard to determine the number of people who might qualify.
Well, all these difficulties can be overcome. The records are there; they just have to be searched. They show when a man enlisted, how long he was in Canada and how long he was overseas. They have been carefully kept and this is not an insuperable job at all. I was amused to hear the objections which emanate from officialdom. I do not mind the officials raising the objections; that is their job. They have to point out to ministers and parliamentary secretaries the difficulties in the way of new legislation, and they are responsible for showing that these difficulties exist. But as far as the government is concerned, it should deal with the difficulties and take the necessary steps to put some new measure into effect, if it is found as a matter of policy to be worth while.
I wish to document statements I have made in support of my bill by actual cases I have

Private Bills
dealt with, where I have felt citizens have been deprived of their rights under our statutes or had their rights unneccessarily withheld for a lengthy period of time. The first document I have is a copy of a letter received by a legal firm in my constituency, and it has to do with an immigration case. It is signed by a deputy minister of that department, and I will just read parts of it:
This application has been held up, pending completion of inquiries into the circumstances trader which certain members of the applicant's family arranged for the illegal entry into Canada of a young Chinese lady under the guise of the applicant's sister.
The letter continues, and further on there is this paragraph to which I object most strongly:
X am quite prepared to authorize the admission of Mr. Wong's wife to Canada, now that the facts with respect to the illegal entry of his "sister" have been firmly established: but before doing so I think I should give Mr. Wong a final opportunity to show his good faith by giving the department a truthful statement with respect to the matters which he has thus far been attempting to conceal.
Then there is another sentence:
If you can persuade him that he should do so, this would go far in re-establishing Mr. Wong's good faith in his dealings with the department and would facilitate very greatly his wife's early admission-
To my mind, the last sentence amounts to something like blackmail. If we were to use it in our business, I am sure a charge would be laid against us. I turn again to the beginning of the paragraph where it is stated: "I am quite prepared to authorize". This is the deputy minister. He does not say "my minister" or "my government". It is the boss of the department speaking. Where do these people get this power? Who gave it to them? We gave it to them. That is why I say we have a bureaucratic dictatorship today and not a government of the people. I heard someone say "the minister", meaning the minister gave him that power. This confirms what I said before; we have lost the authority we had. It also confirms what the minister said the other day-that members of parliament are not important. We see here the same situation as exists in France where the country can run without members of parliament. Maybe we should change this system and save the people a lot of money by not having members of parliament. Let us admit we have a bureaucratic dictatorship.
I have here a copy of a letter where the postal cancellation stamp by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration is the product

of the deputy minister's signature, not the minister's. Therefore, I contend that the most powerful man in the department is not the minister, but his deputy.
I would turn to another department, now, the Department of National Revenue. Some time ago I had a request from one of the local schools to bring into Canada some tuned hand bells which the applicant thought were duty free. Then I received a letter from the department saying they were not duty free. I will not repeat all the arguments used by the applicant or by myself as representative of the constituency to prove that they were duty free, other than to quote a sentence from the last letter I received from the minister. It reads:
The fact remains that tuned hand bells are not provided for in item 696(1). While they may well be instruments, they are not "philosophical instruments" nor "scientific instruments".
I used the department's own terms to prove otherwise. If we look at any dictionary we see that the term "philosophical" means "belonging to or used in the study of material philosophy or physics." Philosophy means reasoned science. There are many definitions of "science", but the fourth one set out in the dictionary I use is this: "any one of the seven liberal arts-grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, music, geometry, astronomy". The definition of "music" is "the science and art of the rhythmic combination of tones." In other words, the department set out those two qualifications, that they must be philosophic instruments or scientific instruments, and when we proved that they were, the answer was still, no.
The next case is a peculiar one. It has to do with the commanding officer of a local unit. To make the story as brief as I can, this commanding officer was let out of his command without cause. A mutual friend asked me if I would try to find out why this officer was let out. After five or six weeks of trying, I finally went to the Prime Minister's office about it and received an answer. I will not read the whole of the letter which was written to me on the subject. The main part of it was to the effect that the unit was in a parlous state, that much difficulty had been experienced with reports and returns, and that the over-all situation was most unsatisfactory. In other words, this officer was a poor administrator. Incidentally, the officer concerned did not know I had endeavoured to find out why he was let out.
When I got this information I went to this mutual friend of ours and said: "You had

better tell him now why he was let out". This was done. At that time, the commanding officer did not really care whether he got the unit back or not. However, when he received this information he became very annoyed and said: "All right. Now they will either put up or shut up". I got permission to go over all his reports and as far as administration was concerned there was not one lower than "good". They were all either "very good" or "excellent".
Most of the transaction was carried on by correspondence. I could see by the reports I was receiving that I was losing my case fighting for this officer. However, that fall there was an army corps conference down here at which a trophy was to be awarded for the best administered unit in all Canada -perhaps I should say "western Canada" to be sure. Lo and behold, the unit under this particular commanding officer won this trophy for the best administered unit. I think that was the clincher. They withdrew what they had said. They said the officer could retain his unit, and they hoped I was satisfied.
I was not satisfied, Mr. Speaker. First of all, the commanding officer would not take the unit back, in the circumstances. Furthermore I, as a member of parliament, had a further point I wished to raise. I had received a reply from the Prime Minister's office-I presume it came from officials in the department-to the effect that the man was a bad administrator, that the unit was in a parlous state, and so on. The men who acted as judges to decide who should win this trophy were not I believe army men, though they had been in the past, nor were they connected with the government. The award was made on a fair basis. In other words, the Prime Minister was getting false information from one of his departments.
My question is this: How can any prime minister run a country if this is the type of information he is getting from the departments? Something should be done about it. Something should be done about the persons who originated the report I have in my hand. When I brought this latter question up, the reply I got about a month later was that the man concerned retired "about 30 days ago."
I have another case here which is peculiar to the west. This concerns an application from one of the ranchers in my constituency -an application to establish a basic herd. This application must be made to the Department of National Revenue. In order to be as
Private Bills
brief as possible, I will just read the reply which this applicant received:
It has been decided that a basic herd cannot be granted, due to the following reasons:
(a)	Insufficient sales shown in the years the returns were filed.
(b)	Possibility that livestock was taken in trade for machinery and claimed as an expense.
Hon. members will note the word "possibility". In this connection I do not think I could do better than quote the reply sent by this man's lawyer to the department. Here is his letter to the Department of National Revenue:
We are absolutely astounded and amazed at the
contents of your letters of the 8th instant	
May we suggest further that before you should be entitled to make the statements contained in your letter which appear to be nothing short of accusations of fraud on the part of our client, there should be some very definite basis for said statements.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING WITHHOLDING OR REFUSAL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
I am sure the remarks of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek will have met with a receptive audience in all corners of the house, not only because of the tone in which he presented his arguments but also from the personal experience of hon. members on occasions in dealing with various aspects of government. It is, after all, one of the most important functions of a member of parliament to try to assist constituents in connection with problems raised by particular administrative decisions which affect them adversely.
The remarks made by the hon. member will find a considerable echo over the years in connection with development which has taken place in Canada, as well as in many other countries, of a body of law referred to as administrative law. It is now more than 50 years since Lord Chief Justice Hewart the former chief justice of the high court in Britain wrote a book entitled "The New Despotism", in which he objected to the very evident growth in Britain and elsewhere in the world of an administrative procedure whereby the rights of individuals were affected, not by decisions of courts of law, which had to proceed upon pre-determined principles and from which there were rights of appeal, but by administrative officers who could not be reached by the law.
It seems to me the objection which the hon. member is making is not so much that

Private Bills
there has been a greater ramification of bureaucracy itself-because if the many measures which find support in this house for increasing activity by the government in all phases of life are to be effective, then inevitably there is going to be an increase in government action and decision making by government officials-but rather his criticism is as to the manner in which these officials act, the manner in which they take their decisions and the manner in which they carry out those decisions. In one of the long standing cases of British administrative law which has been applied by the courts of this country, the case of Board of Education v. Rice, it has been said that the obligation of an administrative official is to act fairly, to hear both sides of any particular question; because after all that is a basic obligation upon anybody who has to decide anything.
Many measures have been proposed in this house, in addition to that proposed by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh), which are directed to the same end. We have had in this and earlier sessions a number of legislative proposals for the introduction of the office of ombudsman. I was interested in the hon. member's reference to a speech made by the New Zealand high commissioner because, as hon. members know, the office of ombudsman has been introduced into that dominion and has, to my knowledge at least, worked effectively. The real responsibility of the ombudsman is to make sure that the administrative decision is taken with an absence of arbitrariness, that it is taken fairly and-as the judge said in the case of the Board of Education v. Rice-that where it is appropriate both sides are heard by the particular official.
There have been other proposals along this line. I recall that there was a proposal by the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) in her maiden speech in this house. The proposal was that we should consider the enactment of an administrative procedure act which resembles, perhaps, that which exists with regard to the federal service in the United States. That, again, might well be a desirable objective, but it will not entirely meet the concern the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek expressed today and which I think is echoed by hon. members. There are many, many areas which cannot be reached effectively by legal process because the decision is not a legal one or is not of such a scale, in terms of either time or money, that it is possible for a court or series of courts to review it.

Another suggestion which has come from many hon. members is that there should be increased research facilities for members of parliament so that, to borrow a vernacular phrase, the rights of any particular constituent will not be buried under a "snow job" by an individual administrator who is in better possession of the facts than is the member of parliament.
I think all these matters deserve attention by this parliament, but I would submit that the particular measure put forward by the hon. member would not be likely to correct this particular wrong, which we all recognize and which many of us feel should be corrected in a variety of ways. My reason for saying so is by reference to the words of the proposed amendment itself. Hon. members will note, in looking at it, that, to borrow a lawyer's term, there is no element of mens rea; there is no element of guilty intent required to establish the offence under the particular section. The offence can be established and the particular official can be punished, and very severely, in accordance with the provisions of subclause (b), by the mere proof that there has been action which deprives an individual of his rights, whether or not action was taken by the official with a completely honest intent, was taken by him because of a genuine and honest mistake as to the law, or whether it was taken by him, again, with complete genuineness, but without being in full possession of the facts. I would suggest that the measure proposed by the hon. member for the purpose of inhibiting oppressive action is itself almost more oppressive than that which it seeks to restrain.
A further problem which arises in this regard is the very obvious difficulty of any administrative officer in determining the extent to which any particular action may or may not accord with the basic guarantees set down by the Canadian Bill of Rights. The Canadian Bill of Rights is modelled very closely, or certainly took inspiration from, the bill of rights which has been included in the amendments to the United States constitution. That constitution is a living document, and for the past 150 years or more it has been the subject of continued and very intense definition by the courts.
I suggest it would be well nigh impossible for any particular individual in any particular instance to determine, for example, whether he was depriving an individual of property or liberty without due process of law. It would be almost impossible for him

to determine whether in any particular instance his conduct did or did not amount to a violation of the Canadian Bill of Rights. While it certainly is desirable, as the hon. member suggested, that there should be fairness in arriving at decisions-and I think all hon. members would support that-I think all hon. members, on reflecting on the difficulty which would be created, would agree that there would be a great risk that the heavy criminal penalties the hon. member is proposing here against members of the civil service, who may be acting in perfect honesty, would result in the civil service in critical areas being paralysed rather than assisted and decision making being impaired by this particular measure. For these reasons I feel this particular legislative proposal is not one that should commend itself to members of this house; it is not one that is appropriate for dealing with this problem.
As to the particular cases referred to by the hon. member, I am sure there may well be problems of the kind referred to but I am not in the position to answer each one individually. However, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that even in those cases there was very probably that honest difference of opinion which, while it might call for administrative action, does not call for the harsh kind of action which this bill proposes.
