speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the course of the discussion this afternoon the subject of the procedure of this house came up for a little discussion. Because like you, sir, I am a member of the special committee on procedure and organization, it was not my intention to raise this matter at this time, and even so the remarks that I shall make will be brief.
The hon. member for Port Arthur said something this afternoon which I hope will be noted. He suggested that perhaps the most important question that faces us procedurally, the most important question that faces us in the management of the affairs of the House of Commons, is this question of planning or allocating our parliamentary time. As our business in parliament grows apace from year to year and as issues which we discuss become sharper, it seems to me that we are going to have to face this problem and come up with an answer to it. I think we should be mature enough to realize that doing some planning and organizing of our debates does not involve the denial of free speech or the down-grading of democracy.
We already have, Mr. Chairman, many rules and regulations which some believe might have interfered with free speech. We have a rule that no member can speak at one time for more than a certain number of minutes. We have a rule that when Mr. Speaker is in the chair no member can speak more than once to the same question. We have rules as to when the house sits and when it adjourns. We have rules that limit the debate to eight days with respect to the address in reply to the speech from the throne and to six days on the main budget debate. In addition to that we have a rule that limits debates on supply motions to two days each. We introduced this year the temporary rule that limits the length of debate on a notice of motion for the production of papers. I do not think anyone would allege

Interim Supply
that because we have these various limitations, in some dastardly way we have denied freedom of speech to members who are elected by their constituents to come here and represent them in parliament. These rules are simply common sense regulations that we have agreed to, so that one person will not talk all the time, so that there will not be anarchy and so that we can get along with the business we have come here to do.
It just so happens, Mr. Chairman, that some of us here feel that the amount of that business has so increased that we are going to have to extend this principle of planning, regulating and organizing our parliamentary time. That is why I think we should put our minds to this problem. That is why I think we should consider it and discuss it and negotiate it in committees and in conferences, and resolve that we will come up with a solution. What some of us have proposed is already in the public domain and I do not intend to refer to it at length. Indeed, what I shall say is offered not in any argumentative sense but rather as an example of one way in which I think this problem can be solved.
I think we could by a standing order provide for a special committee which could make recommendations as to the length of time that would be spent on certain debates. I think we could, if we could agree to such a standing order, reach agreement in advance before a certain debate on second reading, or in committee of the whole or what have you, got started, and having reached agreement could then have the debate end at that agreed point, just as the debate on the address now ends at the end of eight days and the debate on the budget now ends at the end of six days.
It seems to me that by some such process we could introduce regularity, order and some common sense into the use of the time which we have. We have only so much time. There are only 12 months in the year, and the amount of business that we have, if you take into consideration the necessity to spend some time in our constituencies, compels us to plan and organize our business. I hope that we will move to some form of this kind of planning. I certainly do not urge that the particular proposal, the drafting of which I have had something to do with, is sacrosanct; if someone else can draw up a better one, that is fine. But I do plead that we look at this whole problem objectively and realize that, if we can reach agreement on the planning and organization of our time, we are not denying

freedom of speech, we are not bringing down the curtain on democracy; we shall be making the work of this house more effective.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Chairman, we should be honest enough to admit that the criticisms which are made of us sometimes in the press and by commentators are merited. Instead of just saying they are wrong we should pay some attention to them. For example, I think of last night's "Viewpoint" on the C.B.C., wherein James Stewart of the Montreal Star gave his assessment of the debate of yesterday and the previous two or three days. It was pretty critical, and I think it was a valid criticism. I think it is good for us to hear that kind of criticism. But in addition to hearing it, I think we should take it to heart and try to make some improvements in our proceedings.
This afternoon there was obviously a little difference of opinion between some of us in this group about a certain word, the word "closure". I mention it again only to draw the distinction between closure as it is now in our standing orders-it is standing order 33-and the planning or the allocating of our time in the way the hon. member for Port Arthur urged the house to consider. Closure is something which is imposed by the government when it has a majority one way or the other, and it is brought on after a debate has bogged down, after there is ill will and antagonism and all the things which we know have developed on those few occasions in Canadian history when closure has been used. But the kind of thing the hon. member for Port Arthur urged this afternoon on behalf of this group, the kind of thing I have had a part with you, sir, in drafting for consideration of those who were dealing with this matter, is quite different.
What we propose is not that the government use whatever majority it commands to compel the house to quit a debate that has already bogged down. What we propose instead is agreement among the parties through a committee that will consider the matter, and what we also propose is that agreement be reached in advance. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that is not a denial of free speech, not a ringing down of the curtain on democracy. It is something that is sensible, that is a case of planning, a case of organizing the time that we have.
As I have already said this afternoon and repeated when I started this evening, if it

had not been for the fact that the question was opened up I would not be speaking on it, for the reason I already gave. I have the great privilege of being a member of the committee on procedure and organization and we are working hard on this very question. We have been on the question of the allocation of time, or what have you, for over two months. We have had meetings of the main committee and the subcommittee times without number. The proposal I have referred to is before the committee and an alternative proposal was presented by a member of the committee yesterday. We are wrestling with the matter. It is slow business. I do not blame members for being impatient, but because I am involved in the negotiating I should like any remarks I make to be of a general nature rather than a case of indulging in controversy.
But I do support the proposition that the hon. member for Port Arthur put forward this afternoon, namely that this whole question of coming to grips with the planning of our parliamentary time is one of the most important questions that faces us as members of parliament.
Do like we did in Quebec. Get rid of the Conservative party.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
That remark is not consistent with the spirit in which I am trying to approach this question because I think that if we are going to achieve anything of the kind I am advocating it has got to be done by general agreement, almost by unanimous agreement, among the parties and groups that make up the House of Commons. My plea is that we should think about this matter and consider the representations that are being made to us by people outside who criticize our activities, and let us see if we cannot do something along this line.
I say again, Mr. Chairman, that I am as opposed to the use of closure as I was in 1956. I have said on occasion, and I think it is in print in various places, that it is not closure itself that is bad but rather it is the abuse of closure that is bad. That is a nice, academic statement to make, but the fact of history is that every time it has been used since it was first brought in in 1913 it seems to have been a case of abuse. It has always produced a nasty, difficult situation in the House of Commons.
I think we have got to find something better than the stopping of debate by the vote of the majority. I think we have got to find a better way whereby we can get together, bargain in good faith, negotiate and
Interim Supply
come up with a method of planning our business. I agree 1000 per cent with the words used in this connection this afternoon by the hon. member for Port Arthur, that this is the most important problem facing us, and I think we have got to grapple with it. When suggestions are made there is no point in trying to find some easy way out; but we will grapple with the problem if we face suggestions seriously, as we are doing in the special committee on procedure and organization. If some members are impatient with our delay, I accept that criticism on behalf of my subcommittee at any rate. But it may be that if it takes us a little while longer to come up with something, we will produce something that will be lasting and worth while and will help to make parliament a place where freedom of speech remains, but where we will do our job a little more efficiently than is sometimes the case.
If it had not been for this subject being raised this afternoon I would have spoken only on the one other subject about which I now wish to say a few words. I am glad that the President of the Privy Council is in his place, as he has been throughout this debate on interim supply because he is piloting it through the committee and the house. I remind him that on June 11, as recorded on page 4186 of Hansard, he made a commitment as to something he would do in committee of supply.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
This was the second time to my knowledge that the question of ministers having secretaries or employees on the government payroll working in their constituencies had been raised. The first time it was raised was on June 9, as recorded on page 4088 of Hansard. It was raised on that occasion by the hon. member for Red Deer and the President of the Privy Council gave a short answer, but went on to say he would do his best to see what further answer could be brought forward. Then, as I have said, on June 11 the matter was raised by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency. My leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, took part in the discussion. It was obvious that we were not satisfied, and so it was that on that occasion the President of the Privy Council said:
I will be glad to discuss the matter further on interim supply. I do not yet have all the information I want. Since this question was raised in the house I have had the appropriate officials get the

Interim Supply
information and put it together, but it is not complete at the moment. However, I will be able to give more information later.
This question arose because of news reports that got out to the effect that in at least two cases people had been taken on staff at government expense and assigned to offices or places within the constituencies of the ministers concerned. Some of us felt this was a questionable procedure and I for one looked up the Civil Service Act under which we were told this had been done. I am looking at the Statutes of 1960-61, chapter 57, and I find that section 71, subsection 1, reads as follows:
A minister may appoint his executive assistant and his private secretary, and other persons to be employed in the office of a minister shall be appointed by the governor in council.
Surely the key words in that subsection are the words "to be employed in the office of a minister". We learned that there were two orders in council. There may be others, but we know of two. One is P.C. 1964-5/490 which appointed Mr. Andre Cote as special assistant in the office of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration at Baie des Sables, Quebec, with salary at the rate of $7,500 per annum, effective March 2, 1964. The other was order in council P.C. 1964-18/738 which recommended the appointment of certain persons as indicated on the document in the office of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, with salaries at the rates stated, effective May 1, 1964. One of those listed by name is referred to as "principal clerk at Niagara Falls, Ontario", and the salary is $5,220 a year.
I wondered how it was possible to appoint people by order in council to work at these places, one in the province of Quebec and the other at Niagara Falls, in view of the wording in the act which says that such appointments shall be made of persons "to be employed in the office of a minister". That is the reason, of course, that I put on the order paper two rather harmless looking questions. One read, "Where is the office of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration", and the other read, "Where is the office of the Minister of National Health and Welfare". It seemed to me those were very simple questions which could be answered almost immediately. Surely these ministers know in each case where his office is, but it took ten days to get answers to these questions. When the first opportunity went by without the questions being answered I got up on a question of privilege. In reply the parlia-

mentary secretary to the Secretary of State said that there was some difficulty involved, and I quote his words as found on page 4399 of Hansard:
-the delay here Is due to the problem of Interpreting the precise meaning of the word "office". Does this refer to the place, or does it refer to a particular legal function performed by the minister? When this question has been dealt with, the answers will be forthcoming.
Well, a week later, on June 24 on page 4661-62 of Hansard, we got the answers as to where these offices are located. In the case of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, this is the answer:
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration performs the duties of office in various places, but principally at the following addresses: Citizenship building 22-30 Slater street, Ottawa: 439C, House of Commons, parliament buildings; and second floor, Immigration building, Champlain harbour station, Wolfe's Cove, Quebec.
Now, how can one stretch the words "can be employed in the office of the minister", to offices in the plural? I point out also, that unless my geography is completely lacking, I do not see any connection between Wolfe's Cove and Baie des Sables. In other words, there is no attempt in the order in council to suggest that this person is employed in any one of the offices of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
In the case of the Minister of National Health and Welfare this was the answer given on June 24:
The Minister of National Health and Welfare performs the duties of her office in various places, but principally at the following address: Copeland building, Ottawa, Canada; room 253S, House of Commons, Ottawa, Canada; 551 Clifton avenue, Niagara Falls, Ontario.
Well, it is very obvious, Mr. Chairman, that the reason for the delay in producing answers to this simple question was to produce something that would fit the facts that had been brought out in the meantime. But the fact still remains that the act under which these orders in council were produced speaks of the office of the minister in the singular. I will read it again:
-other persons to be employed in the office of a minister shall be appointed by the governor in council.
I suggest that it is just playing with the law to say that, on the basis of that, persons can be employed anywhere in the country where the minister says, "This is a place where I am doing the work of my office". What is "office"? Is it a function or is it a working place, the place where people are employed?

If this is true, I want to give some information to the Leader of the Opposition, if I could have his attention for a moment, because there is a subsection in this same section 71 that happens to deal with him. Subsection (5) of section 71 says:
This section applies to a person employed in the office of the person holding the recognized position of Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons as it applies to a person employed in the office of a minister.
Now, Mr. Chairman, if what the government has done is valid, all the Leader of the Opposition has to do is say he has an office in Prince Albert, that he performs his work at offices in various places, say in the House of Commons and in the home that is provided for him in Rockcliffe, in Prince Albert or wherever he chooses, then under the same provision he can get, at government expense, clerical or secretarial help in his office. Now, mind you, the law does not go any further but fairness would go further. If a minister can have people on the government payroll in his office in his constituency, if the Leader of the Opposition can have this help, then the member for Cape Breton South should have clerical help at an office in Sydney or Glace Bay. I have an office at 1036 Notre Dame avenue, Winnipeg, and I should like to have some help there.

If the hon. gentleman would allow me, I would say he does not tempt me. I was not tempted when I was prime minister, and paid my own office expenses. I am not tempted now, but it is a very interesting observation.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition is such a good Baptist, I knew there was no point in putting temptation in front of him.
I am always able to resist.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I trust that Hansard got his words, that he is always able to resist.
We are having a bit of fun about this. Even this last bit of fun that has been raised is not inappropriate. If it is fair for a minister to have assistance with his work in the constituency, it is fair for a member. The amount of work is growing so that this is becoming a real issue. Perhaps we do not need the same amount of help, but I suggest we need help if we are going to do our job effectively and efficiently. If it is fair and proper for some people to have this kind of help, then the provision should be extended to all.
The point I am making now, Mr. Chairman, is not the question of extending it but the question of the validity of those two orders
Interim Supply
in council. They are purportedly based-they say so-on the provisions of section 71 (1) of the Civil Service Act; both of them name that section. I have read the section. The section says people can be employed by order in council in the office of a minister. The ministers have stretched things a bit by telling us they have several offices. However, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has not even told us he has an office at Baie des Sables, Quebec.
One of the reasons given by the President of the Privy Council for following this practice was that the former government did it; it had been done down through the years. The President of the Privy Council said that one change had been made. Previously, it had been done by a minute of the treasury board, and now it is done by order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, it is the very opposite.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I see the minister shaking his head.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should like to be quoted accurately. Perhaps I can help the hon. member if he wishes. I will help him clarify the point he is making.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member asked me to read his words. There is a slight difference between what I said and what he said. He did say one change had been made. I am quoting now from page 4185 of Hansard for June 11, 1964;
The practice of appointing persons to the staffs of ministers outside of Ottawa is a long established practice which goes back many years. When this government took office it reviewed the practice followed by the previous administration and continued to maintain it in force. There was one change; now the appointments have to be approved by the treasury board before the order in council is submitted to the governor in council.
I thank the hon. member for suggesting that I read it correctly. What does that one change amount to? The fact is it is still being done by order in council, supposedly based on a particular section of the act. If I understand the meaning of words at all, surely that meaning is clear, that the persons to be employed in the office of the minister shall be appointed by the governor in council. But the ministers do not know where their offices are. Having appointed these people to offices in their constituencies, then they try to come up with a definition that includes this. I suggest that is playing with the law. This is not good. The law is something very serious, and I think that the government, of all people, should pay attention to the strict observance of the law.

Interim Supply

Mr. Chairman, I was not going to take part in this debate, but since the subject has turned to what I consider a more sensible point of view, particularly in connection with the house, its rules and procedures, I would like to say a few words.
I am a relative newcomer here and have not been aged in the parliamentary process that is apparently so much required. I agree to a great extent with what the hon. member for Port Arthur said, that the house is here to protect the rights of individuals, to debate principles and legislation and to supply money to the government, but I wonder whether the people of the country think we should be doing more in the way of legislation.
Quite recently many comments were made about the other place. It would probably surprise hon. members to know that the work done there by the members of the other house is probably more than has been accomplished here, and they have given more knowledge and initiative to the people of Canada than we have given. Indeed, I think it is time we must consider whether we should not change and drastically reform the rules under which we work.
This is going to require the wisdom of Solomon because, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, if limitation is put on debates-and in all likelihood this will be organized by the whips-then my chance of getting to speak will be very slim, as will be that of the hon. member for Port Arthur. On the other hand I do agree with the hon. gentleman from Winnipeg North Centre when he says we must make some attempt to plan the order of business of the house. If we are going to do that however, we shall have to plan a little deeper than we have up to now, and I say this with the greatest respect. The only example I can use is that of the question period, which used to take anywhere from an hour to an hour and a half. A decision was taken to postpone part of it, but it still takes an hour and a half, and we have that second question period as well. We have not done very well in that reform.
It is said hon. gentlemen ask questions because they do not know the answers. Of course this is not so. If they did not know the answers they would not ask the questions. They know the answers quite well. In this void of activity in the house we have come to a new era where the establishment has grown. What is the establishment? Well, it is difficult to define, but its power is easily

felt in anything we do. Indeed I would say that most of the comments, most of the barbs aimed from the other side in this debate have not been so much at the ministers but at this establishment, and that includes the comments during the last few days about the film. The establishment is that body which decided to keep these people incarcerated for some 90 odd days. It is not the minister; it is that overpowering establishment, without control.
I know the ministers and what they do. Analysing very clearly the duties they have, even if they work a 16 or 18 hour day, when a minister gets through with the interviews, cabinet meetings and the house-he must sit in the house-and the speeches he is expected to make, he has not got time to find his office, as the hon. gentleman who _ preceded me pointed out, let alone try to initiate the program of the government. Consequently this has now been transferred to the establishment.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question. Would he explain what he refers to as the establishment. What does my hon. friend mean-and I may say I refer to him very truly and sincerely as my hon. friend.

I am just trying to point out that the establishment is difficult to define, but it is administration gone rampant-is that what you might call it? It is these people who have made the decisions, the administration with the powers they have assumed, and they have done this in the past, and not just with the present government. I do not think it has come about all of a sudden. It is a growing thing and it is going to be hard to straighten out.
The legislation should initiate here. This is a most able house. In private life I have had some experience in business, and I will say without hesitation that most of the members here would do credit to any enterprise that they choose or would have chosen in the business world. It is unfortunate that there is no means of expression in the house. The talents here are obvious, and I speak of every corner of the house, but they are now being used to split hairs, to debate rules of procedure, points of order, which party should sit closer to the Speaker, and whether one member was enticed from one party to another. These are the things in which the members have to interest themselves, because there is so little room for expression.

We have had a very good example of how the talents of all hon. gentlemen were used in the special committee on defence, a very good committee which has helped the minister. We all acknowledge the minister had very little trouble with the house, and that he had a great amount of help and assistance from members in all parties. Since we have had this good example I ask why the committee on rules and procedure could not consider this as another way of extending the work that is available, possibly with committees attached to every department from which the ministers can get advice in initiating legislation-not from the administration, not from the establishment, but from the members elected by the people of Canada.
I have the greatest respect for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who is heading the committee on procedures, but I sometimes wonder whether he truly agrees with me on what reform is. Consider, Mr. Chairman, the page boys just behind you, possibly a throwback from Nelson's flagship. These young boys walk right by our noses every single day, but have we stopped to consider that they get on their buses at 11.30 at night and do not get home until midnight? They have to go to school in the morning, at seven or eight o'clock, and they can only spend a half day at school.
How many of them drop out and what have we done for them? If we must have page boys let us see that they get an education, that possibly they be tutored. Have we become so callous, so hard that we do not even notice these things. My idea of reform is that the nation can no longer tolerate these lads going through life without an education.
I had this happen to me the other day. A page boy who was becoming too old to be a page boy came to me to see if I could get him a job in the Department of Public Works. But he had only received a grade VII education and the civil service would not take him. We have done this. We should consider carefully, if we are to have page boys, whether they are to be educated and whether they should be given the same opportunity as we would give to our own children. This, indeed, would amount to reform, and it is on this note that I would like to conclude.
Carried.

It is curious, but it always seems that when anyone on this side wishes to speak we are urged to go a little faster,
Interim Supply
but when someone else, over there, wants to speak it does not matter if time is taken up.
I have been extremely touched by the charges coming from the government side, especially from the Prime Minister, that the business of the house has slowed down to a crawl-that there is obstruction. Well, what hypocrisy. That is all I can call it. I sat on that side of the house for five years and watched the four horsemen at work, as well as those people behind him. They can still teach this side some lessons on how to slow things down to a crawl. There is no point in recrimination. I am not going to say "yes, you did" or "no, you didn't". But I will say that it lies ill in the mouth of the government at this time to say we are not getting on with the business of the house.
Let us look at the committees situation. This year committees were not called until April 10. They did not meet for organization until April 21. In the past, under previous governments, the estimates committee had at least one, if not two departments to get through. This administration has not referred one department to the estimates committee. It has not sat-oh yes, it did sit, for an organization meeting. Since then it has not done a thing. Oh, the hon. lady, who I see in her place, did come in at the last minute. I was a member of that estimates committee and I have gone over the estimates of many a department. Many departmental estimates could have been referred to other committees. Why, for instance, have not the estimates of the Department of Labour been referred to the committee on industrial relations? The committee on marine and fisheries could have handled the estimates of the Department of Fisheries. The estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce could have gone to the estimates committee, as well as those of the Minister of Justice, the house leader himself. We could have done something. Instead, everything has been held back. The government cannot say that the departments have not been called. We have had four supply motions and the estimates are available. If hon. gentlemen opposite would listen to some of their own officials they would know that many senior officials welcome the opportunity to go before the estimates committee or a special committee because it gives them an opportunity of putting forward their opinions and reviewing their position, thus developing the administration of government. Instead, everything is kept in the enclave of the treasury bench.

Interim Supply
Let us look where some of the faults lie. It is not so much in the legislation. We have not seen any legislation of any consequence. The representation bill has been hidden away since April 27. What legislation has been blocked? The government would like to get to the flag resolution. Well, I will read what John Meyer, financial editor of the Montreal Gazette has to say about the introduction of the flag resolution at this stage:
Matters erf present concern to the conduct of business have now been put aside in favour of what will be prolonged and acrimonious debate on the flag. This is a luxury the country is not yet in a position to afford.
I will tell those on the treasury benches this: They ought to see what their reputation is like abroad. I have come back after three weeks spent talking to Canadians and friends of Canada and they say: What on earth has gotten into your government, that they should go forward with this sort of proposition at this time? Hon. gentlemen opposite may frown. The Minister of Trade and Commerce may frown in disbelief. But if it were not a breach of confidence with the people who told me these things I would give him the names. I do not intend to go into the flag issue right now, but I will say this: Do not go crying on anybody's shoulder or shedding crocodile tears about the business of the country.
Student loans, the revision of the family allowance plan, the pension act, the legislation dealing with rail transportation-all these things are ahead of us. We remember on May 15 the Prime Minister reading that long list of parliamentary business. He impressed on the house and on the country at the time the importance of dealing with all these things before the summer recess. Then he put that little caveat at the end. And what did we get? We got the flag resolution. That will settle the country's affairs. This is the kind of priority we were given. It was nothing but a political sham to introduce it at this time. We could discuss a flag-and I am quite prepared to do so on a later occasion this year, when we have dealt with these other matters. Has it priority over the pension plan in the scheme of affairs of this country? Has it priority over the growing need for a change in our transportation set-up or any of those other matters which the Prime Minister impressed upon us as being highly important. They have been thrown in the ash can. Even so, does the Prime Minister think that when he proposes, we should dis-

pose without question of a matter such as the flag issue? Did he or his advisers think for one moment that they would get away with a picayune debate in this chamber? If so, they are sadly mistaken. Certainly the Liberals have gotten much further away from the grass than they were in 1956 and 1957.
I suggest to the house leader that even now there is time to pick up some of these loose threads. Why does he not have estimates referred to the estimates committee? The members are prepared to work. I have here a list of what has been done by the various committees. The committee on agriculture and colonization, organized on April 21, has met to discuss tobacco research. The committee on banking and commerce organized on April 23 has dealt with some bills which came to it from the other place. The miscellaneous private bills committee has done the work assigned to it. The industrial relations committee was organized on April 23 and as far as I can see it remains organized. The veterans affairs committee was organized on April 21 and it has stood down. The committee on food and drugs, a special committee, is carrying on. The committee on procedure and organization, a special committee, is carrying on. The committee on marine and fisheries was organized on April 30 and is dealing with pieces of legislation. The public accounts committee was organized on April 30 and is working. The committee on mines, forests and waters was organized on April 30 and is standing by. The committee on privileges and elections has had its days in court. Next, railways, canals and telegraph lines. It has been dealing with the reports of the crown corporations connected with transportation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: What about external affairs?
External affairs met earlier, and it has dealt with the Columbia river treaty. Yes, it worked. And it is dealing with the estimates.
We are waiting for the estimates.

My hon. friend from Oxford tells me they are waiting for the estimates. Why haven't they been meeting? Item 1 was discussed in the house and the debate was adjourned so that the estimates could go to the committee. Is this organization of the business of the house? You do not have to have any wide revision of the rules, just to bring in new rules to break or not observe. If we observed the rules that we have, we

could do a good job. Half the speeches could be much more relevant, and that would cut down the time taken.
Hear, hear.
Well, you can always hang a little bait and the suckers will bite. I will tell you who are the chief offenders.
You are.
The chief offenders are the ministers in their opening statements. They open the shop wide.
Oh, oh.

I think I have a little experience in this regard and I will say this; I am not singling out the speeches from the opposition side or the government side as being particularly irrelevant. This is a criticism that applies to us all. I suppose this afternoon we have indulged in a little bit of confessing of one's soul, and therefore I would ask hon. members to look at their own speeches and see that they are relevant; that on second reading they are not making the speech they could not make at the resolution stage, or that on clause 1 in committee they are not making the speech that the whip did not allow them to make on second reading.
I can see that some of the younger members on the other side of the house seem to think that at the present time things are not all as they should be, and they feel gagged, frustrated. I ask them and those who have sat over here to just read the previous Hansards and they will see that some of their colleagues who are now silent-they are the proverbial mummies-when they were over here were the gadflies of Hansard. It all depends on what side of the house you sit as to how you look at it.
I am going to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that in regard to this question we should ourselves pay a little more attention to the rules and let the government organize its business. Let us see some of these estimates go to committees; let them have more estimates. We can have estimates for two days a week. I fully subscribe to the remarks of my colleague from Winnipeg South Centre, and I would say that the principal task of this house is to grant supply and to examine government administration and business. That is done in the consideration of the estimates.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I would like to pass on to one or two other matters. If the Minister of Justice is within earshot I would like to address to him a personal plea. In 1962 there was introduced in the
Interim Supply
other place Bill No. S-2, dealing with amendments to the Bankruptcy Act. It was passed in the Senate, given first reading in this house and then that parliament was dissolved. Last year the present administration brought forward the same legislation. It was amended in the Senate and brought here and given first reading, but has died. This is important legislation in certain provinces which are seeking these changes to the Bankruptcy Act. My prime concern is this. I do not know what happens in the minister's office. Has he a great big sack for correspondence that is almost bottomless, because I have written and written to his office but have received no reply. I think that I, as a member of this house, am entitled, just like any other member, to the courtesy of a reply. I am not putting the blame entirely on the minister; but surely to goodness somebody in that circle of assistants who have been hired is at fault. These letters of inquiry on government business should receive an immediate reply. I asked a very simple question: Is it the government's intention to reintroduce this legislation: and if so, when? Yet, Mr. Minister, two letters, the first dated May 6 and the second May 20, have gone unacknowledged. I regret that I have to say this publicly, but it is something that must be corrected.
There is another point I would like to raise with the Minister of Justice. This also dates back to 1962. I had correspondence with his predecessor in this regard and I have had correspondence with him. This is a very technical point from a lawyer's point of view, but I think it is a rank injustice that it continues to exist. I refer to the abrogation by judgment of the former president of the exchequer court of rule 264 of the rules of that court, dealing with the taxation of solicitor and client costs by the registrar. It has been in the rules for many years and solicitors have advised their clients on it; parties have acted on the strength of it. A right is established under this rule. We know in the common law provinces that we can do this: If a client is not satisfied with my solicitor's bill on a conveyance, that bill can be taxed before a taxing officer. There is thus some justice; he does not have to start a supreme court action or a district court action, nor do I have to start such an action to get my bill established.
In an unreported judgment back in 1961 this rule was declared to be ultra vires. I am not going to go into the merits of that judgment as to whether this should or should not be the case, but I think the procedure was

Interim Supply
wrong. First of all, I think it is wrong that the judgment should be unreported, and second I think it is wrong that no remedial action has been taken to amend the Exchequer Court Act to take care of this situation. The president of the exchequer court indicated that the act did not provide for this, and that therefore it was ultra vires. Correspondence with the ministers of justice has indicated that they are considering changes to the Exchequer Court Act. I would like to see the appropriate action taken. It is not a very complicated matter and action could be initiated in the other place. May I commend this to the Minister of Justice, because I think a grave injustice is being done to a great many clients, particularly those in the case on which this judgment was based.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would like to turn my attention to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in the few minutes that remain at my disposal. This question is concerned with the application of section 5(d) of the Immigration Act, the so-called statutory bar. We know that in the past there were many cases in Hong Kong where a wife took a false statutory declaration in the furthering of a scheme for the entry into this country of her husband. As a result of the investigations which were conducted, as a result of the amnesty that was granted to all persons of Chinese origin in this country who might have entered illegally-that is, if they had come forward, disclosed all the facts and had their status regularized-these people were told by the minister in a letter, which thanks them for their courtesy and co-operation in so coming forward, that they now enjoy full status as though they had arrived here legally in the first place. They then applied for their wives, and the answer was immediately given: "We regret that she cannot enter this country because she took a false statutory declaration and is therefore barred under section 5(d) of the Immigration Act". In other words, the minor partner or accomplice in a scheme, which is, it is admitted, an illegal scheme, is the one who is punished after the principal actor has entered the country and been forgiven. Or is there just a delayed penalty behind the minister's letter when he says to them: "Your status is as though you had entered this country legally and you have the same rights as anyone else, with the exception that you cannot bring your wife to Canada for five years after she had taken the statutory declaration"?
I have written to the minister in regard to a number of cases of this kind and I

would urge upon him an immediate revision or review of the application of the statutory bar. I realize the necessity for regulation; but in view of the fact that this amnesty has been given, why visit a further penalty upon these people? After all, I should think in 99 per cent of such cases the wife has been a docile accomplice. She has been asked to take this statutory declaration in order to fit the scheme. Yet we are visiting an additional penalty upon her while her husband, who is here, has been forgiven and goes scot free. I would urge on the minister that this matter be reviewed immediately.
The last matter I should like to speak about, Mr. Chairman, concerns Canadians who travel abroad in Europe and our Canadian personnel in our embassies in Europe. Do you know, Mr. Chairman, what they have to read for news of Canada? They get, provided the Telex is not overcrowded, a sort of synthesis of a C.B.C. news release, a daily edition but necessarily compressed to perhaps one page or a page and a half foolscap size. Then they get the first four pages of Le Devoir, which are cut out and air mailed. Then the Ottawa Journal makes a special print of the four principal pages-the front page, the editorial page and a couple of other pages-and sends them over. Then there is available a sort of business overseas edition of the Globe and Mail. For the people in external affairs there may be certain confidential bulletins, but they are confidential. But beyond that they must depend upon the European edition of the New York Herald Tribune, the New York Times, or the continental edition of the London Daily Telegraph for news about Canada. I found all our personnel right from the top down, starved for news of Canada. The armed services do a little better. There are two Yukon passenger flights plus four freight flights a week, and they are able to obtain daily copies-sometimes a little delayed by reason of flight schedules-of the Globe and Mail. These arrive at Marville, France. So they have at least one newspaper.
I went into one Canadian embassy in Europe and the latest daily newspaper, outside of those I have mentioned, was an April edition of the Montreal Gazette. Other than that our personnel have to rely upon their own subscriptions.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I could raise a point here and put it in the form of a question to the hon. member. Important as is the matter he is discussing- and I recognize its importance-I am wondering whether he is satisfied that it is the type

of problem which should be discussed on interim supply, which is a temporary measure asking for one month's supply for the government to carry on its business until the regular estimates come before the house. I am wondering whether it is not the type of subject, bearing in mind the practice on interim supply bills, which could not better be discussed on the estimates of the department when the minister is here.

Mr. Chairman, this is all very well on the part of the President of the Privy Council, but I would like to say that in the time the minister has taken I could have completed the point I wanted to make.
Carried.

The estimates of the Department of External Affairs will come up in anno domini-some time, perhaps in the fall. I am interested in getting some action now in response to the suggestion I am going to make.
Carried.
I think that what the government should do is to provide for a reasonable number of daily papers from across Canada to be sent to our embassies via the regular service flights which go to Europe.
Carried.

Certainly these people are quite as entitled as anybody else to have news about Canada. Europe is crawling with Canadians right now who are hungry for news about Canada but cannot get it.
I suggest we also provide a litter to carry out the hon. gentleman who is hollering to be carried out.
I trust that the ministers concerned will take to heart the suggestions I have made.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to make a few remarks relating to a matter of great concern to a number of my constituents. I rise primarily on account of a telegram I have received from the president of the B.C. command of the Canadian Legion and the local branch to which I belong, as well as a result of resolutions passed by the zone council of the Royal Canadian Legion for Kootenay West. However, before doing so I want to say that while there has been considerable criticism as to the length of debate with respect to the historic "Mr. Pearson" film incident, I suggest this debate would have been considerably shortened had the Prime
Interim Supply
Minister made the speech he made yesterday some years ago.
Oh, oh.

No, pardon me; it seems so long ago since it started. I should have said, had he made the speech some days ago, the debate would have been considerably shortened.
I return to the subject which I wish to speak on for a few minutes this evening. I do so because of the telegrams I have received and because I believe the federal government has a responsibility to the persons concerned, in view of statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. During the discussions in the external affairs committee with respect to the Columbia river treaty, and later while the minister was speaking in the house he indicated that the government was quite assured that the persons who would be directly affected as a result of the flooding would be properly treated. In that respect I want to quote what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in the house when dealing with this question. He said, as found on page 3903 of Hansard:
The immense magnitude of the program is most apparent, as are the changes in the face of the land that are bound to take place.
That is no overstatement.
It was known from the beginning that, regardless of what sequence of development was chosen, the changes would be of such magnitude that the face of the land in the Columbia basin would be altered, that immense areas would have to be flooded, that there would be dislocation and that new conditions of living would be imposed in that region. However, there had to be the assurance in the minds of the negotiators, both federal and provincial, that although these changes were necessary the benefits would be far greater and sufficiently great to justify the changes both in the land and in the lives of numbers of people. There had to be the assurance that no one would suffer loss, that there would be alternative programs of settlement and redevelopment on available lands, that there would be redevelopment of communities affected together with compensation to those who would suffer loss sufficient to provide them with a stake sufficient to re-establish themselves.
I re-emphasize those concluding words of the minister when speaking in the debate at the time the house ratified the treaty. Then I go to the minutes of the external affairs committee and I wish to quote what the famous Dr. Keenleyside had to say as found on page 405:
Here we have said from the beginning, and in this we have had the full support of the British Columbia government, that we propose to treat these people fairly, sympathetically and generously?

Interim. Supply
Quite recently the famous Dr. Keenleyside attended public meetings at Edgewood and Nakusp on the Arrow lakes at the request of the local residents. In the first instance he intended to attend only dinner meetings of chambers of commerce, nice, cosy meetings where you do not meet the people. But the people sent him letters demanding public meetings. I give great credit to the women of my constituency who organized these public meetings. Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that if you get the women in the constituency on your side you have already won. They organized a large public meeting and Dr. Keenleyside was subjected to a barrage of questions from the property owners in the district with respect to the clearing of the basin, with respect to the relocation of roads, the relocation of wharves, the relocation of schools and other community facilities, with respect to the compensation to be paid to the owners of properties to be flooded and with respect to the provisions for the restoration of fisheries which as a result of this flooding will be destroyed for a period of over 20 years.
As a result of the meeting the people were most dissatisfied. Dr. Keenleyside completely failed to answer the questions satisfactorily at this large public meeting in that district. As a result of one meeting one property owner wrote to the B.C. hydro and power authority with respect to the policy to be followed in connection with compensation and so on, and I am going to place the reply on the record:
This is a copy of a letter received from R. W. Gross, manager, land division, B.C. hydro, in answer to the queries of a landowner in the district.
"Dr. Keenleyside has asked me to acknowledge the receipt of and reply to your letter of 20th of April. I am afraid we cannot accept the principle that replacement value is to be paid for improvements affected by the Columbia developments. The basis on which compensation is paid in Canada for private property required for public purposes is clearly established on the value to the owners principle.
Value to the owner is in almost all cases the same as market value. In addition to market value there would, in proper cases, be added an allowance to cover disturbance and moving expenses.
You ask the question, "Why should anyone be forced to go Into debt to replace what they now have"? It might help you to understand the situation if you appreciated that all privately owned property in Canada is held by its present owner subject to the right of any public body possessing power of expropriation to take it over for public purposes.
I want to bring those words to the attention of the great advocates of free enterprise.
In these circumstances the public body is required to pay the owner what his property is worth, not what it may cost him to replace it.

The owner is entitled to be left in the same economic position in terms of cash or property after the taking as he was in before the taking. An owner is not entitled to profit from the taking, which would be the situation if replacement value rather than market value were paid."
I bring this to the attention of the house because it is a complete contradiction of the statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and Mr. Keenleyside to the committee and also in numerous addresses throughout the country, that these people would be treated in a humane and generous manner. This has caused a great deal of concern to the 2,000 odd people who are going to be affected by this development.
As a result this question was considered by a recent zone council convention of the Royal Canadian Legion representing all branches in Kootenay West. I see the hon. member for Kamloops looking at me and I hope he will begin to stand up for these people and their rights. This matter has caused a great deal of concern, because to get the market value means in many cases, in view of the flooding that is to occur, to get a fraction of what will be required to relocate these people on farms similar to those they now occupy. I received a telegram from the zone council of the Royal Canadian Legion, representing all branches in Kootenay West, which telegram reads as follows:
Sir: The following resolution was duly adopted at the west Kootenay zone convention of the Royal Canadian Legion on June 21st, 1964.
"Whereas the veterans residing in the flood basins of the Columbia river, who are to be affected by the treaty, will be at a disadvantage negotiating with trained officials of the B.C. hydro authority and whereas experience has shown great variance in allowance for similar properties received from hydro authorities for similar areas for no apparent reason, and whereas these affected veterans are in fact negotiating for the interests of Veterans Land Act, National Housing Act, soldier settlement board and others as well as those of their own;
Therefore be it resolved that the honourable minister of the Department of Veterans Affairs be asked to provide immediate professional assistance to veterans affected by the hydro developments of the Columbia river treaty projects."
In addition, Mr. Chairman, I received a telegram from the branch of which I happen to be a member and which I had the honour to organize in 1919. It contains a resolution passed at the zone convention on June 21, 1964.
With regard to displacement to persons living in the area to be flooded by the Columbia development projects whereas it has been stated, in verbal and written form by Dr. H. L. Keenleyside, that market value will be the criterion used in the purchase of property of affected persons and whereas the use of market value can mean a very great hardship on people who cannot afford to pay

the difference between market value and actual cost of replacement and whereas many veterans will be affected, and suffer hardship by the system of market value settlement; Therefore be it resolved that the Royal Canadian Legion support the principle as follows, when a person or persons are faced with the necessity of having to move, where a cash settlement is not suitable, that the hydro authority resettle such persons in accommodation not less favourable to them, at no cost to persons so resettled.
This telegram is signed, F. E. Sadd, secretary of the branch.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this matter is of serious concern to some of these veterans, owing to the circumstances of the district where up to the present time there are few paved highways, where most of the areas are served by country, gravel roads. Many of these people are isolated. The assessed values are somewhat low because they have not had the expensive government services. However, I know of one case where one of these ranchers ships $40,000 worth of cattle per year to the market. Just imagine what will happen to that man if he receives, say, twice the assessed value of the property plus 10 per cent for inconvenience. In that case, I know from personal experience, it would cost in the neighbourhood of $100,000 to buy a similar property.
I know several ranchers in the district, veterans particularly, where in some circumstances these persons have spent their life in this work, and in some cases their fathers have spent their lives, and they are entitled to most generous treatment when they are being displaced by a work for the benefit of the people of Canada. I object most strongly on their behalf to the suggestion made by Dr. Keenleyside of the B.C. hydro, as expressed in the letter that I have quoted. The people who attended this public meeting at Edge-wood and Nakusp were very dissatisfied with the answers given by the co-chairman of B.C. hydro to the numerous questions they raised.
I have been asked to raise this question at the first opportunity. This is the reason I bring it to your attention tonight, Mr. Chairman, and to the attention of the house. I appeal to the Minister of Veterans Affairs to appoint some official to go to these veterans who live along this 150 miles of beautiful waterway, the Switzerland of North America, where there are 50 miles of beaches to be destroyed to provide a water tank for the United States, to give assistance and advice on their legal rights. I know the parliamentary secretary is a very humane sort of person. I trust he brings this situation to the attention of the minister and that the departinterim Supply
ment does appoint someone to represent all these veterans, whether they hold property as a result of purchasing it from the Veterans Land Act administration, from any other agency of government, or whether they purchased their property outright.
In concluding, I say this, that men who have fought for Canada are entitled to be protected by the federal government in circumstances like these and not subjected to, shall I say, the legal, cold blooded treatment it appears they are going to receive from the B.C. power and hydro authority.

Mr. Chairman, I did not plan on speaking tonight until I had to listen to a couple of speeches from the leaders of the minor parties accusing us of holding up legislation in this house. I shall come back to them later.
First, I should like to call the attention of this government, as I have attempted to do on several occasions, to what I refer to as the master agency plan. I believe this plan brings hardship and injustice to western Canada. I raised this problem with the former minister of transport, but did not get any reply from him. I went to the board of transport commissioners with regard to the closing of these stations. I could not get satisfaction from the board of transport commissioners. Many communities in western Canada have lost the services of the station agent, and this is bringing difficulty to the people. If I may give an example, about two weeks ago I sent a telegram from the city of Saskatoon to my home. I went 300 miles on the train and beat the telegram to Irma. In another instance, some people in Irma had friends coming to visit them. Those friends sent a telegram and they also beat the telegram to Irma. This is an example of what is happening. We can get no support whatever from the board of transport commissioners. They are just political appointees and are not serving the public. I think we might as well dispose of the board of transport commissioners, because the railways go ahead and do what they want anyway.
Now, the matter of this government and its policies was well covered by the hon. member for Edmonton West. speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Earlier this evening, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised the question of the appointment of ministerial staff. He raised two aspects of this matter. First, he reminded us that on June 11, the day before we first presented this resolution for the consideration of the house, I had undertaken in answer to some questions asked by his leader and by others to discuss this subject on interim supply. The other point he raised concerned the legality of certain aspects of appointments by order in council.
Perhaps I might dispose of the legal question first. The hon. member quoted section 71 of the Civil Service Act and sought to argue on this basis that the appointment or employment of any staff of a minister outside Ottawa was illegal. I would simply point out to the hon. member that he has misinterpreted the section he has read. If he would read the whole of the section he would realize, surely, that the word "office" as used in the section refers to the office of the minister, or the minister's establishment as separate from the administrative branch of the department. The Civil Service Act deals, of course, with both types of appointment or employment. That is the distinction which has to be drawn.
The word "office" as, I think, will be apparent to anyone, is used in two or three different contexts. It may mean the physical location of a room or set of rooms in which a person works. The other meaning has to do with a position to which certain duties are attached; a place of trust, authority or service, especially of a public kind. I would think that this latter definition of the meaning of the

word "office" as taken from the Concise Oxford Dictionary is the obvious meaning of the word as used in the section.
Without developing this argument further I would, therefore, point out to the hon. member that his deduction as to the legality of the appointment is not the correct one. I might say that when he raised this point some days ago I immediately looked at the section myself-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I wonder whether the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) is giving at present a legal advice on a section of the act or the statutes of Canada. If this is what he is doing, I suggest that the President of the Privy Council will also have to tell us who has given him this legal advice and, if so, whether this legal advice comes from the Department of Justice in Ottawa.

The hon. member for

Having looked at the section myself, and having come to that conclusion, and having reinforced my view of it by turning to the Oxford dictionary as to the meaning of the word "office", I then asked my colleague, the Minister of Justice, for an opinion on the matter and he, as is his responsibility, or duty, did give me an opinion; and it was along the lines I have indicated.

speechtext:
Well, I have been in the chamber during the whole of the time this interim supply resolution has been before the committee, and I am quite ready to answer all the questions I can. I did promise the house that I would answer some of the questions that were asked a few days ago on this whole subject, and I would like to do that now.
The stationing outside Ottawa of members of the staffs of ministers of the crown is

Interim Supply
consistent with past practice and has considerations of economy and efficiency to support it. From the records, it is clear that ministers have maintained members of their staffs at places outside Ottawa since 1935- and I do not know how far back the practice does go, but that was as far back as I was able to get the records-and possibly for many years before that. Ministers have traditionally maintained offices in federal public buildings in cities like Montreal, Quebec city, Toronto, Vancouver and Winnipeg.
And Matane.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In 1956-57, six members of ministers' staffs were employed in Vancouver, Windsor, Montreal and Lunenburg. Under the Conservative administration the number of members of ministers staffs working outside Ottawa was doubled. During the period 1958 to 1963, 12 persons were employed in Regina; Hamilton; Fredericton; St. Gilles, Quebec; Montreal; Middleton, Nova Scotia; Brandon and Mont Laurier.
And Matane.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
At present there are 15 persons employed full time and one person part time at ministers' offices at Quebec city, Bathurst, Montreal, Toronto, Sorel, Niagara Falls, St. Boniface and Vancouver.
It is interesting to note that the Glassco commission has recently pointed out that only 24 per cent of the full time federal public service work in the Ottawa-Hull area. Three quarters of the public servants are dispersed throughout the rest of Canada, largely in 14 urban centres from St. John's to Victoria. As the Glassco commission observed, "How these scattered activities are organized and staffed, how their performance is appraised and their effectiveness ensured are matters of importance to the economy and efficiency of the federal administration and to quality of service received by the public". The commission asserted that "more systematic and energetic measures are needed to encourage the freer movement of public servants between headquarters and field establishments".
Since the Civil Service Act, 1961, the staffs of ministers of the crown are appointed in accordance with section 71(1) of the Civil Service Act. That section reads:
A minister may appoint his executive assistant and his private secretary, and other persons to be employed in the office of a minister shall be appointed by the governor in council.

The function of certain staff members who are provided for ministers of the crown, and for the leader of the opposition, is to relieve these ministers and the opposition leader from certain routine tasks and thus enable them to discharge more effectively their ministerial and public responsibilities. The posting of a member of the minister's staff to a centre outside Ottawa, whether in the minister's constituency or in some other area, has been found to improve the efficiency of service to the public and to reduce claims for travelling expenses. Under the present administration, no members of ministers' staffs stationed outside Ottawa are drawing an expense account.
To ensure that members of ministers' staffs fulfil their responsibilities of assisting the ministers and do not merely undertake routine political tasks on behalf of party or local organizations, the present government has already instituted the practice of requiring that proposed appointments be reviewed by treasury board before going forward to the governor in council for approval. In its review, treasury board ensures that the total size of a minister's staff, wherever located, remains within reasonable limits bearing in mind the size of the departmental organization.
It is not as simple a question as it may seem whether there should be a rule that all members of the staff of ministers should be obliged to live in Ottawa. This has not been the rule in the past. It may well be that ministers could be relieved of much of their obligation to deal with the manifold problems of their constituents by a secretary or a stenographer living in their constituency at a good deal smaller expense than would be the case if that employee were obliged to live in Ottawa.
I must add, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister has instructed treasury board to examine into the whole question of ministerial assistants working outside Ottawa. He has asked treasury board to report on how this practice, as it has developed over the years, can be brought under strict control so that abuses, if any, can be prevented, and whether there are any advantages to the public service under the practice which should be retained under the control referred to.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister sits down could I ask him if he could have some information ready for us in the morning regarding the 15 full time persons and one part time person presently employed

by ministers outside Ottawa. Perhaps he could tell us the locations and in how many cases these persons are actually located in the constituency of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I would be very glad to give that information. I would point out that there are very, very few of them in the constituencies of the ministers; they are mainly in the major cities. But I will have that detailed information as soon as I can get it. I should point out, also, that there is a possibility of slight inaccuracies in some of the earlier information because I have had to reconstruct it as best I could from old orders in council, departmental records and things of that sort.

Mr. Speaker, during the question
period I asked the leader of the Quebec Liberals, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) a question.
As the province of Quebec has about 38 per cent of all Canada unemployed, I asked him whether he would use his influence to obtain from the government that the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials be abolished, not only to help the economic recovery of the province of Quebec and favour the building

Mr. Speaker, we have to face not only winter unemployment but summer unemployment as well, and I may say that, so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, building activities have decreased by at least 60 per cent, in comparison to former years, and just because of that 11 per cent tax.

The housing contractors are roused and alarmed. Building is decreasing; the number of bankruptcies is constantly on the increase, more particularly in the building field, because the profit margin is very slim at this time, more particularly since the government imposed that famous 11 per cent tax, which runs counter to every economic principle. Mr. Speaker, I recognize and respect the hon. member's concern for unemployment. This government has been greatly concerned about the employment situation in Canada, and contrary to what was done by the previous government has indeed done a great deal about it. If he will reflect over the past year, there has been the extension of the winter works program, the extension of vocational training assistance, the $500 housing bonus paid for winter building, the program with regard to designated areas, including the three year tax holiday, the two year write-off on machinery, the five year write-off on buildings, along with double depreciation that has been granted on new equipment across the whole of Canada. I think the people agree that this government has done a good deal with respect to unemployment. Indeed, the success of our program is shown by the fact that unemployment in Canada is now lower than it has ever been since the last time that a Liberal government was in power.
The hon. member's attempt to relate unemployment to the sales tax extension is, I maintain, entirely unwarranted. There has been a great expansion of building in Quebec and in the whole of Canada. I challenge him to support the figure he just quoted of a 60 per cent reduction in construction in Quebec. I should like to refer the hon. member to my speech of February 25, 1964 in this respect and also to the Financial Post of February 22, 1964.
I should also like to refer him to the publication, National Accounts, Income and Expenditure, for the first quarter of 1964, published by the dominion bureau of statistics. I quote from page 3 thereof:

-the value of residential construction put in place in the first quarter was about 25 per cent higher than in the preceding period.
I quote further from page 7:
Spending on fixed capital, including housing, provided the major impetus to production in the first quarter and the rise of 11 per cent carried total capital expenditures to an annual rate of $8.8 billion after discounting seasonal factors.
If the hon. member will recall, I stated in my speech on February 25, 1964 that such expenditures would amount to $8 billion this year and I am pleased that that figure is going to be surpassed and will reach $8.8 billion, almost the biggest construction year in Canada's history. I quote further from the same page of the report:
The demand for business fixed capital absorbed 19 per cent of gross national product compared with 17 per cent in the first quarter of 1963. The annual rate of housing completions rose to an unsurpassed level of 215.8 thousand in the first quarter as the final qualifying date for the government's winter housebuilding incentive bonus was approached.
